To address this limitation, power modeling has emerged as a promising but challenging solution. This work introduces a novel, automated methodology for fast and cycle-accurate power modeling of embedded processor cores. The key innovation lies in using a minimal feature set mainly based on processor control signals, which significantly reduces modeling overhead. To ensure generality, we employ a residual-based model that combines linear regression (LR) and decision tree (DT) techniques to capture residual error information, making the model highly adaptive to unseen data. To obtain a power model, we explore the modeling space across various modeling alternatives, evaluating their performance in terms of accuracy and modeling effort. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves a cycle-by-cycle power prediction error of less than 3% and a simulation speed of 6.6 Mcycles/s. The proposed methodology is integrated within an automated framework, streamlining both dataset generation and model training processes. This automation ensures efficiency and scalability, significantly reducing manual effort for the IP developer.

item.title: Behavioral Modeling of RF-Input DLMBA Based on Optimized DVR Model Using Improved PSO Algorithm
item.description: This work presents a behavioral modeling methodology for a recently reported multitransistor power amplifier (PA) utilizing a novel architecture, as a radio frequency (RF)-input divisional load-modulated balanced amplifier (RF-Input DLMBA). Due to the active nonlinear load modulation between multiple active devices, this type of PA exhibits significant nonlinearity, as well as memory effects that are difficult to model using traditional techniques. An improved particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm with dynamic nonlinear self-adaptive hyperparameters (DNSHs) (PSO-DNSH) has been employed for the threshold optimization of the decomposed vector rotation (DVR) model in this work. An introduction to the basic principles and modeling procedures of this proposed technique is provided. RF-Input DLMBAs, which are designed in-house, have been used for modeling and digital predistortion (DPD) validation for different output powers, signal bandwidths, and back-off ranges. The results indicate that, compared with traditional models and standard PSO-based DVR models, better prediction performance has been achieved by the proposed model.

item.title: ULTRA-MACE: A Unified Low-Bit Trans-Precision Reconfigurable Multiply-Accumulate Compute Engine for Accelerated Computing
item.description: The rising demand for energy- and resource-efficient edge-AI platforms calls for compute engines that balance throughput, flexibility, and run-time efficiency under tight bandwidth constraints. This brief presents ULTRA-MACE, a unified low-bit transprecision reconfigurable multiply-accumulate compute engine (MACE) that supports FP4 (E2M1), FP8 (E4M3), Posit-(8, 2), and Posit-(16, 3) through a six-stage vectorized pipeline with 128-bit quire accumulation. ULTRA-MACE employs a high-precision split mantissa multiplication scheme and an integrated gated bypass for ReLU, achieving $4\times $ / $2\times $ / $2\times $ / $1\times $ throughput (FP4/FP8/Posit-8/Posit-16) without increasing bandwidth demand. Postroute results in 28 nm CMOS demonstrate a peak energy efficiency of 12.8 TFLOPS/W at 0.9 V and a compute density of 8.2 TFLOPS/mm2. Integrated into the TREA accelerator with 64 MACE, the FPGA prototype achieves 89% of theoretical peak performance and maintains practical accuracy with only 1.5% degradation relative to the FP32 baseline. Overall, these results demonstrate an efficient transprecision compute engine for edge-AI acceleration.

item.title: Cheerful: Hardware-Oriented Early Exits for Ubiquitous Computing
item.description: Variations in the computational capabilities of edge devices and runtime resource availability pose considerable challenges in developing efficient ubiquitous inference. Dynamic neural networks (DyNNs) have been developed to address device heterogeneity by adapting network structures or parameters to complex deployment environments. However, existing DyNN methods are largely insensitive to runtime resource variations and hardware-specific configurations, and their reliance on extensive profiling complicates deployment. In this work, we present Cheerful, a hardware-oriented, ubiquitous early exit (EEx) framework that enables efficient inference on heterogeneous devices by combining hardware-parameterized performance modeling and optimization with online adaptation to resource variations. In the offline stage, Cheerful models key performance metrics by integrating comprehensive analytical and data-driven methods, formulates an optimization problem to achieve the tradeoff between inference accuracy and energy cost, and incorporates hardware-specific parameters to accommodate device heterogeneity. In the online stage, Cheerful integrates a lightweight hardware-aware inference engine (HIE) that jointly adjusts early exit configurations and CPU frequency based on run-time resource availability, using dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). Extensive experiments on heterogeneous devices demonstrate that Cheerful outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the accuracy–energy Pareto frontier in resource-constrained environments while maintaining low deployment overhead.

item.title: On Maximizing Quality-of-Service of Mixed-Criticality Systems With Energy Constraints
item.description: Energy consumption plays a crucial role in battery-powered mixed-criticality systems (MCS). However, recent research has not considered energy consumption as a strict constraint. In this article, we focus on the processor speed allocation issue of MCS with energy constraints, with the goal of maximizing the quality-of-service (QoS) of low-criticality (LO) tasks in the high-criticality (HI) mode. First, this problem is formulated as a nonlinear optimization problem. Second, we propose a simple heuristic algorithm called ASHA to solve this problem on unicore platforms. The ASHA algorithm first calculates the maximum utilization of LO tasks in HI mode and then uses the greedy algorithm to assign the compensating factor of LO tasks. Third, we extend this solution to multicore platforms. Finally, experimental results indicate that our ASHA algorithm performs more effectively on a unicore platform, while the criticality-unaware worst-fit decreasing (WFD) algorithm shows better performance on multicore platforms.

item.title: A Universal and Lightweight Automated Design Framework for Multiband Power Amplifiers
item.description: In power amplifier (PA) design, the repeated trial-and-error process and time-consuming electromagnetic (EM) simulation are major obstacles to achieving efficient design. In this study, based on a small microstrip line (ML) dataset, a lightweight deep neural network (DNN) is trained to accurately predict the S-parameters of layout-level matching networks (MNs). Leveraging the DNN’s high-speed prediction capabilities and an ordinary particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm, the entire optimization process is completed without the involvement of EM simulation software, enabling highly efficient automated design of PAs. This method is applied to the automated synthesis of narrowband, triband, and broadband PAs, demonstrating high flexibility. Among these, the broadband PA (a 0.5–5-GHz gallium nitride (GaN) PA) is fabricated for validation. Measurement results show that within the operating frequency range, the output power reaches 39–42.2 dBm, and the drain efficiency (DE) ranges from 47.2% to 74.6%, with an average of 56.5%.

item.title: DIONet3D: Dual-Input Dual-Output Deep Neural Network With 3-D-Enhanced PDN Feature for IR Drop Prediction in 3-D ICs
item.description: Accurate IR drop analysis in 3-D integrated circuits (3-D ICs) is critical for ensuring power integrity and physical design convergence. However, conventional IR drop simulation flows suffer from extensive runtime and complicated flows, making them difficult for early-stage design evaluation and large-scale design iterations. To address this challenge, we propose DIONet3D, a novel dual-input dual-output neural network tailored for IR drop prediction in 3-D ICs. DIONet3D takes feature maps from both top and bottom dies as input, incorporates a shared backbone with U-Net structure, and outputs IR drop maps for both dies simultaneously. To enhance the modeling of 3-D power-delivery effects, we introduce a physics-guided 3-D-enhanced power delivery network (PDN) representation, in which planar PDN stripes are converted into spatially continuous features through Gaussian kernel-based smoothing, while vertical hybrid bonding (HB)/through-silicon via (TSV) connections are encoded to capture cross-die power delivery. This hybrid representation enables the network to capture both interdie and intradie features effectively while balancing the computation efficiency and feature representation efficiency. Furthermore, a compound loss function is proposed, combining multiple loss functions with dynamic weighting to balance multitask convergence and improve structural consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) methods and achieves good generalization performance. Compared to commercial EDA simulation tools, DIONet3D achieves high structural and spatial similarity, with up to $309\times $ runtime speedup and $89\times $ memory reduction under CPU inference. Our results demonstrate that DIONet3D offers an accurate and lightweight surrogate solution for 3-D IC IR drop evaluation.

item.title: HEIRS-PS: Hybrid 3-D RRAM- and SRAM-CIM for Pipelined Sparse Multitask Transformer Acceleration
item.description: Multitask transformers have garnered widespread attention for fast task adaptation at edge. However, in addition to matrix–vector multiplication (MVM) with static and dynamic weights in the data-intensive transformer, task adaptation introduces new challenge of weight updating. Besides, while sparsity can help mitigate the rapid growth in parameter size and computational demand, it requires great hardware flexibility. Compute-in-memory (CIM) is widely explored to overcome the memory bottleneck in neural network acceleration, mainly with single type of memory devices, but struggles to balance the storage density with computing flexibility across multiple tasks. Meanwhile, the conventional pipeline parallel dataflow for high throughput suffers from the underutilization with bubbles caused by variable input sequence length and model sparsity. In this article, HEIRS-PS, a hybrid three-dimension RRAM- and SRAM-CIM architecture, is proposed for the pipelined multitask transformer acceleration with sparsity. With the 3-D integrated RRAM-CIM and SRAM-CIM arrays, a novel hybrid-CIM paradigm is proposed with the collaborative addition to achieve both high storage density and computing flexibility for multitask inference. Moreover, by fully leveraging the hybrid-CIM structure in HEIRS-PS, a new dynamic workload scheduling method is proposed with a layer regrouping method to balance the computing latency across pipeline stages. By eliminating the bubbles, the model inference latency is reduced with higher throughput. Experiment shows that the proposed HEIRS-PS architecture improves the energy efficiency by up to $13.3\times $ and $8.68\times $ , compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) RRAM-CIM and SRAM-CIM works on Llama-1.3B. Moreover, HEIRS-PS also reduces the computing latency by up to 29.5% with the balanced latency across pipeline stages.

item.title: BSDiT: Bit-Serial Diffusion Transformer Acceleration With Dynamic Rotating and Adaptive Step Quantization
item.description: In recent years, Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have emerged as a powerful class of models for visual generative AI, enabling high-fidelity and diverse image synthesis. However, their practical deployment—especially in energy- and resource-constrained environments—is severely hindered by the substantial computational and memory demands introduced by their iterative denoising process. Posttraining quantization (PTQ) is a promising solution to alleviate the heavy memory and computation requirements. However, PTQ for DiTs face significant challenges due to their unique activation and weight characteristics. To address these challenges, we present BSDiT, a holistic algorithm–hardware co-design framework that integrates dynamic block rotation, adaptive step quantization (ASQ), and bit-serial computation to enable accurate and efficient low-bit inference for DiTs. At the algorithm level, BSDiT introduces two key innovations: 1) an outlier-aware dynamic rotating quantization (DRQ) that mitigates activation quantization errors by adaptively redistributing channel-wise magnitude variations and 2) an ASQ scheme that preserves numerical fidelity of weights under aggressive bit-width reduction. At the hardware level, we co-design a bit-serial accelerator with a lightweight rotation engine and a unified dequant-outlier processing unit that efficiently handles both outlier computations and dequantized accumulation within a single pipeline. Furthermore, we develop a dedicated weight decoder and a bit-serial processing element (PE) tailored to the proposed step-based bit-sparse (SBS) encoding. Experimental results show that BSDiT achieves better accuracy than the state-of-the-art DiT quantization methods. When implemented as a custom accelerator, BSDiT delivers up to $3.04\times $ speedup and $3.41\times $ energy reduction compared with leading DiT accelerators.

item.title: LIMCA: LLM for Automating Analog In-Memory Computing Architecture Design Exploration
item.description: In this brief, we introduce LIMCA, a novel fine-tuning-free large language model (LLM)-driven framework for automating the design and evaluation of in-memory computing (IMC) crossbar architectures. Unlike traditional approaches, where the manual, knowledge-intensive design process and the lack of high-quality circuit netlists have significantly constrained design space exploration (DSE) and optimization to behavioral system-level tools, LIMCA employs a no-human-in-loop (NHIL) automated pipeline to generate and validate circuit netlists for SPICE simulations, eliminating manual intervention. LIMCA systematically explores the IMC design space by leveraging a structured dataset and LLM-based performance evaluation. Our experimental results on MNIST classification demonstrate that LIMCA successfully generates crossbar designs achieving $\geq$ 96% accuracy while maintaining a power consumption $\leq$ 3 W, making this the first work in LLM-assisted IMC DSE. Compared to existing frameworks, LIMCA provides an automated, scalable, and hardware-aware solution, reducing design exploration time while ensuring user-constrained performance tradeoffs. Artifacts are open-sourced at https://github.com/ACADLab/LIMCA
